Close MikeHur's Diary Wandering Around: a browser game that turns OSM into a walkable world Posted by MikeHur on 3 November 2026 in English . Last updated on 8 November 2026. I’ve been building Wandering Around , a free browser game in which you can walk around any town or city on Earth. The whole world comes from OpenStreetMap, so I’d like to share how it uses OSM data and ask this community for feedback. Play it here: https://wanderingaround.games (works on phone and desktop, no account needed) News and updates: https://ko-fi.com/wanderingaroundtheworld Screenshots and a short video: https://mikehur.itch.io/wandering-around How the map is built Streets, buildings, water, parks and bridges come from OpenFreeMap vector tiles (zoom 14, OpenMapTiles schema). The game fetches the tiles around the player, decodes them in the browser, stitches buildings that are split across tile edges and turns everything back into OSM-style features with tags. The game logic works on those tags, so it is the same code whether the data comes from tiles or (as a fallback) from Overpass. 2D and 3D: the same data drives a 2D map and a 3D eye-level view. Building heights come from OSM where they are tagged. Transit: train routes and stations, city buses, ferries and signposts come from Overpass queries, so you can travel between real stops and stations. pages.text: Misclassification of Employees as Independent Contractors Under the Fair Labor Standards Act | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content Misclassification of Employees as Independent Contractors Under the Fair Labor Standards Act A worker is entitled to minimum wage and overtime pay protections under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) when there is an employment relationship between the worker and an employer and there is coverage under the FLSA. Employers are responsible for determining whether a worker is an employee under the FLSA. Misclassification occurs when an employer treats a worker who is an employee under the FLSA as an independent contractor. Misclassifying employees as independent contractors is a serious problem because misclassified employees may not receive the minimum wage and overtime pay to which they are entitled under the FLSA or other benefits and protections to which they are entitled under the law. As part of its efforts to address misclassification, the Wage and Hour Division on January 10, 2024 published a final rule , effective March 11, 2024, revising its guidance on how to analyze whether a worker is an employee or independent contractor under the FLSA. This guidance is available in the form of regulations at 29 CFR Part 795. Employers and workers may consult these regulations and the additional resources listed below to help analyze a worker’s status as an employee or independent contractor under the FLSA. Monitoring Surface Water Chemistry Surface water chemistry is a direct indicator of the effects of acid rain on water bodies. Networks that monitor surface water chemistry over long time periods provide valuable information on aquatic ecosystem health and how water bodies respond to changes in acid-causing emissions. EPA oversees the Long-Term Monitoring (LTM) program, which tracks changes in surface water chemistry in response to changing air pollution and acid deposition. The goal of this long-term program is to track whether the Clean Air Act Amendments (CAAA) ( Plain English Guide to the Clean Air Act ) have been effective in reducing the acidity of surface waters in New England, the Northern Adirondack Mountains, Appalachian Plateau, and the Central Appalachians and advance the science of air pollution impacts on water resources. What are Acidified Surface Waters? Acid precipitation (commonly known as acid rain) primarily affects sensitive bodies of water, which are located in watersheds whose soils have a limited ability to neutralize acidic compounds (called “buffering capacity”). pages.text: More Than Money | National Geographic Paid Content for Western Union SCIENCE More Than Money Learn how innovation is helping people support family and friends across borders with greater confidence, flexibility, and choice. 12:59 Every day, money travels thousands of miles across borders, currencies, banks, and financial systems. VIDEO BY NICELY DONE PRODUCTIONS By Sam Kent Last updated November 6, 2026 Food has a remarkable ability to connect us to our heritage. For Sandra Salcedo, who moved from Colombia to Madrid eight years ago, that connection is folded into every pastry she sells at her bakery—a place where people can come together to share memories, stories, and of course, a taste of home. But food isn’t the only way Sandra maintains her connection with Colombia. Thousands of miles away, her uncle Byron relies on the money his niece sends home every month. For Byron, who is unable to work due to illness, Sandra’s contributions help pay for everyday essentials, while providing greater stability for tomorrow. Like millions of people supporting family and friends across borders, she is helping create opportunities that extend beyond a single transfer. As Sandra explains, the money she sends home is her way of being there, and of keeping her uncle company. In her own words: “It represents peace of mind.” Sandra’s story is part of a wider global tapestry. Every year, more than 280 million people send hundreds of billions of dollars home to support the people they left behind. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. https://www.nist.gov/blogs/taking-measure/my-research-working-toward-pain-free-mammogram-alternative Taking Measure Just a Standard Blog My Research Is Working Toward a Pain-Free Mammogram Alternative May 20, 2026 By: Kathryn Keenan Share Facebook Linkedin X.com Email NIST researcher Kathryn Keenan tests a low-field MRI machine adapted to capture breast imagery. The long-term goal of this research is to create a pain-free, accurate alternative to mammograms. Credit: M. The Clean Air Act identifies two types of national ambient air quality standards. Primary standards provide public health protection, including protecting the health of "sensitive" populations such as asthmatics, children, and the elderly. Secondary standards provide public welfare protection, including protection against decreased visibility and damage to animals, crops, vegetation, and buildings. Periodically, the standards are reviewed and sometimes may be revised, establishing new standards. The most recently established standards are listed below. In some areas of the U.S., certain regulatory requirements may also remain for implementation of previously established standards .
